BBC, 24 Nov 16:18 GMT

PM declines meeting with Stormont ministers over budget stalemate

It is understood the prime minister has backed the secretary of state continuing to lead talks on behalf of the government

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, standing outside No 10, wearing glasses, a dark grey suit, grey tie and white shirt.

The Prime Minister Andy Burnham has turned down a request from Northern Ireland's first and deputy first ministers for a meeting over Stormont's budget stalemate.

Michelle O'Neill and Emma Little-Pengelly jointly wrote to the prime minister seeking the direct engagement in a bid to resolve the seven-month impasse.

But it is understood the prime minister has backed Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant continuing to lead talks on behalf of the government.

The prime minister is said to be urging the Stormont executive to accept the government's offer of an extra £1.5bn over the next three years and finalise a financial plan.

No budget has been agreed by Northern Ireland's four-party coalition more than seven months into the financial year.

With no agreement in place, public services have been operating under contingency arrangements – allowing departments to spend up to 95% of last year's funding.

But Stormont ministers have insisted the additional £1.5bn funding offer does not go far enough to enable them to set a budget.

First Minister Michelle O'Neill asked Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly to join her in seeking \"direct engagement\" with the prime minister

First Minister Michelle O'Neill on Monday said she had asked Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly to join her in seeking \"direct engagement\" with the prime minister.

The Sinn Fein vice-president said it would be a \"dereliction of responsibility\" if the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) minister refused.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson appeared to reject the suggestion due to the continuing fall-out between the two parties over the Drumcree parading dispute.

Last month the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in the executive, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the parading row.

But it emerged on Tuesday that Little-Pengelly had agreed to the joint communication.

The deputy first minister claimed her counterpart's request was \"more about a political stunt\", saying it was \"leaked\" to the media \"almost before I could even consider it\".

But Little-Pengelly added: \"I will always do whatever I can to try to secure a budget for Northern Ireland.\"

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said \"fair funding\" was needed from Westminster to support Stormont departments

Speaking to reporters at Stormont, the deputy first minister said she was \"not surprised\" the prime minister would decline a meeting.

\"I think it was always clear that Chris Bryant was the lead in relation to these budget negotiations,\" she said.

Little-Pengelly said the DUP had been \"engaging with the prime minister throughout\" and would \"continue to do so\".

She said \"fair funding\" was needed from Westminster to support Stormont departments.

\"We want our public sector workers - our teachers, our nurses, our doctors - to get the same pay settlement as those working in those areas in Great Britain. That is what is fair,\" she added.

Earlier, the first minister said there had been a \"good discussion\" at an executive meeting on the budget and the \"need to fight for more resources here\".

O'Neill said that \"time is running out in terms of setting the budget\" and public sector workers \"deserve to have their pay awards\".

On her proposal to hold a meeting with the prime minister, she added: \"We're not asking for special treatment - we're asking for fairness.

\"And the fact is that we are underfunded, and he needs to hear that directly from myself.\"

Neon signs made for Stanley Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut film were among the props that went under the hammer in south-west London last week.

God's Own Junk Yard also had pieces made for Tomb Raider, Bridget Jones's Diary and Elton John for sale on Thursday at its workshop on Lots Road, Fulham.

Matthew Bracey, from the family-run business, says materials used to make traditional neon are becoming harder to find as LEDs take over.

He believes neon could be worth more than gold in 10 years' time.
